blocks.text: "Abu Walid," says Pococke, pp. 84–85, "whom we judge the most ancient of the grammarians among the Jews that we possess, has خطوطها [khuṭūṭuhā], their furrows, by which he understands الخطوط التي يخطها الزارع بالسكة بعد البذر [al-khuṭūṭ allatī yakhuṭṭuhā al-zāriʿ bi-l-sikka baʿda al-badhr], those which the farmer draws with his ploughshare after the grain has been sown, which are, he adds, like خدوش في الارض [khudūsh fī al-arḍ], scratches in the ground. And to the same effect he says again in another place (under the root פרד) that they are so named تشبيها بالخدوش [tashbīhan bi-l-khudūsh], on account of their likeness to scratches or wounds made in someone's skin by the nails, which are breaks in the skin. R. Tanchum uses almost the same word, so that for him too תחת מגרפותיהם is תחת חרושהא, under their scratchings, [III, 302] i.e. تحت الخطوط التي يحفرها الحراث التي كانها كسور في الارض [taḥta al-khuṭūṭ allatī yaḥfiruhā al-ḥarrāth allatī kaʾannahā kusūr fī al-arḍ], the furrows (lines) which the plough digs, which are like ridges in the earth; just as elsewhere (Psal. LXV, 10.) they are called, on almost the same principle, גדודים, incisions (our furrows), from גדד, to cut. For this meaning they seek support from the word אגרוף, which occurs in Exod. XXI, 18., and which our people and others, both Jews and Christians, render fist, but which for them (Abu Walid under the root גרף) is شادخ كاسر [shādikh kāsir], something that wounds or makes an incision, كل يجرح او يشدخ به [kull yajraḥ aw yashdakh bihi]. Meanwhile it is evident that by these lines or scratchings (as they call them) we are to understand not hollowed and open furrows but ones covered with earth, drawn through it by the plough or harrow, since the word joined to it, תחת, under, necessarily requires this. Accordingly Aben Esra explains it by העפר, dust or earth, and Kimchi by חתיכות העפר, fragments or particles of dust; hence our people, with most of the more recent interpreters, render it clods. Some try to confirm this from the Arabic language, in which جُرْفٌ [jurf] is said to signify a clod of earth which water rolls along or carries off with it, so that it could be used for any clod. From the root of this word, Hebrew גרף and Arabic أجرف [ajrafa], which means both to roll together and to carry off or scatter, a noun could perhaps not unsuitably be derived denoting earth broken, poured over, rolled together, or thrown upon the grain by plough or harrow; the sense 'clod' being confirmed by الجرفة [al-jurfa], meaning a piece of broken bread, and so perhaps certain fragments or broken pieces of some other thing, such as clods of earth. There remains another explanation of the word, mentioned by the author of an Arabic manuscript (although he expresses it by the Hebrew word itself, مجارفهم [majārifuhum]), namely انادر [anādir], which designates either granaries or heaps of grain in granaries, التي منها يجرف القمح ويودا الي الصحرا [allatī minhā yujraf al-qamḥ wa-yūdā ilā al-ṣaḥrā], from which the wheat (or seed) is removed (or turned away, or taken away) and carried into the field to be committed to the earth, so that this root has the same notion as the preceding, namely of taking away or removing. Grotius reports that some have taken it in this way, rendering heaps, as if the seeds or grains had been spoiled and made unfit for sowing already in the heaps into which they had been gathered." — Since Arabic مِجْرَفَةٌ [mijrafa] is a mattock, or an implement of that kind, suited for throwing out dung or sweeping away dust, Michaelis in Supplemm. ad Lexx. vol. II, p. 361, holds that Hebrew מגרפה too should be taken in the same sense, and renders our words: the grains diminish under the chaff. This sense, already meagre in itself, cannot be admitted also because he takes עבש in the sense of contracting or diminishing, which it has in no cognate dialect. But much more to be rejected is the interpretation of Eckermann, who renders this clause: the things set aside (from פרד, to separate) vanished on account of the chaff (תחת, because of, on account of, as in Ierem. V, 19.), i.e. because what had been set aside in the barns was continually consumed together with the chaff.

"But either Bochart himself," says Pococke, p. 87, "is mistaken here, or the copy he uses is corrupt. For in all the copies, printed and manuscript, that I have happened to see, other words are added to those cited which complete the sense and reveal his meaning to be the contrary: after the words מפני הגשמים, because of the rains, there is added: שלא ירדו עליהם כי גם כן תהיה עצירה גדולה בשנים האלה, which will not come down upon them, for there will be a great drought (or want of rain) at that time."
